title: The Game We Change
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 28 of 40
content:
I beat Iroh at Pai Sho because he underestimated how stubborn I could be.

He would later claim that he had been studying an advanced strategy. I would later point out that his advanced strategy involved staring at the wrong tile for an entire minute.

The board sat between us in the Jasmine Dragon's back room. Rain had cleared the street, leaving the paving wet and dark. Mina had gone home on time. The shop's accounts were finished. For once, nobody was waiting for Iroh to be a general, a mentor or a supplier of tea.

"Your move," I said.

"I am considering."

"You've been considering long enough for the moon to change its mind."

He smiled and moved the white lotus tile. I took it with a move he'd shown me the week before.

His eyebrows rose.

"That," he said, "was not polite."

"You taught me the rule."

"I did not expect you to remember it so enthusiastically."

We played on. He told me stories between turns, and I knew enough about him now to recognize when he was using one to distract me from the board. A story about a merchant who tried to sell fake jade lasted exactly as long as it took him to set up a trap on the far side.

I saw the trap.

"You know," I said, "telling me a story while setting a trap doesn't make the trap invisible."

"An observation of great insight."

"Stop flattering me. It gives you away."

He laughed and, for the first time all evening, actually looked surprised by my next move.

We had planned a relaxed game. Then a knock sounded at the rear door. Ren, the White Lotus scholar, stood in the hallway with a folded note.

"I'm sorry," she said. "The message arrived late."

Iroh took the note but did not open it immediately. "Is anyone in danger?"

"Not at present. The next meeting needs a new room."

"Then I will answer in the morning."

Ren nodded. She had learned to ask; he had learned that an invitation wasn't a command. Once she left, he put the note face down beside the kettle.

"Are you angry with her?" I asked.

"No. She had a reasonable request."

"And you said no."

"Not no. Tomorrow."

I glanced at the board. "A very advanced move."

"One I have been practicing."

We went back to the game. He took my best piece and apologized so extravagantly that I suspected another trick. I leaned across the table to see the far corner and noticed him watching me rather than the tiles.

"What?"

"You look happy."

"That's because I'm winning."

"Ah. So that is what happiness looks like."

"It's a rare experience for you."

He placed one hand over his heart. "Cruel."

I wanted to kiss the smile off his face, which was inconvenient because he was doing his best to win. The moment made me think of the first time I'd sat in this room and mistaken his warm patience for the absence of loneliness. He could be wise and silly and competitive. I liked the silly part more than I'd expected.

The board grew crowded. Iroh could have won in three moves if I'd followed his usual pattern. Instead I traded a piece he considered valuable for a route he'd left open.

He stared.

"Did you mean to do that?"

"Yes."

"You gave up the center."

"I wanted the outside."

He leaned back, then laughed properly. "You are very difficult to teach."

"Try being loved by me."

"I am."

I felt heat in my cheeks. "That's not fair. You can't say something like that when I'm trying to concentrate."

"Perhaps I have developed a strategy after all."

We finished the game. I won by a narrow margin, and he made me recount the move that had changed it. He listened as though it mattered. I didn't need him to pretend to lose, and I didn't need to win to be sure he enjoyed my company.

As we packed the tiles, he asked about the people I would visit next week.

"I'll be going through the Threadway on Thursday," I said. "I've already told you the days. Do you want a note when I arrive?"

"Only if you wish to send one. I would like to know you're safe. I do not need an account of every person you see."

I nodded. Our agreement about ethical non-monogamy and my preference for polyamory wasn't a single confession that solved everything. It was a pattern of choices, like returning to a game after an argument and discovering you could still surprise each other.

Iroh held out the last tile. "One more round?"

"Are you prepared to lose again?"

"Not in the slightest."

I set the box aside. "Then I'm going to claim my prize first."

"And what is that?"

"A kiss, if you want one."

His smile changed. "Very much."

He met me halfway across the table. We bumped the kettle with our elbows and had to stop laughing before we tried again. The kiss that followed was quiet enough to make the laughter seem far away.

Later we went upstairs and closed the door. The board remained on the table, unfinished for the next game. In the morning, I found the white lotus tile at the center and a note in Iroh's careful hand: *A rematch is requested. No tricks promised.*

I put it in my pocket and went downstairs to help open the shop.
